chapter: Bennie Moten, Basie and the Reno
title: Moten's death on the operating table and Dr. Bruce
summary: Goodwin and Smith say a slip of the scalpel, not a heart attack, killed Moten after Bill Saunders brought him back from Denver; Bruce left for Washington.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: About this operation, I do believe that if Dr. Bruce had had any inkling that there was something like this going to happen, I don't think he would have even --

I think he would have turned it over to somebody else to perform the tonsillectomy because he loved Benny and Dr. Bruce was a fine physician, he was a fine man. He did like musicians and this is the last thing in the world that he would have wanted to happen to Benny Mother but I guess it was just -- I guess this could have happened if he hadn't been out the night before. It's just one of those things that happened.

Well, as I understand it, the band was in Denver and Bill Saunders, the great tenor saxophone player, with whom we've all played at one time or another or who has played with us, brought Benny back to town for that operation.
What you're saying is that when Bill and Benny got to town, Benny and Dr. Bruce went out on the town that night --
Not too much out on the town but Dr. Bruce was a person who loved nightclubs. He was in nightclubs every night and he loved Benny but really I think my first time --

Well, what happened? As I understand it, a vein was cut during the operation, because a tonsillectomy is a fairly simple operation, and a vein or an artery was cut and Benny died on the operating table at the age of 35 --
-- which would indicate a mistake was made on the part of the surgeon.
The books say that he died of a heart attack on the table but all you Kansas City jazz musicians say that's not so. What you say is that a mistake was made on the operating table.

It was an accident, a slip of the scalpel. That's the only way I can term it. Now this was -- I wasn't there in the hospital when it happened but this is the version of what most people had said and during the time that it happened. Well, I remember that Dr. Bruce was very low about the whole thing, you know, and it just seemed like it took everything out of him.
He didn't stay in Kansas City much longer. He went to Washington, D. C.
